recent.comment: D beat E, not the better-normalized deep candidates. E’s early-only LN leaves three unnormalized SiLU residual blocks; attenuation of input-dependent features is a plausible explanation for its loss to shallow ReLU D, but was not measured. I overextended normalization/depth preferences from K1006/K1074; K1008 helped identify C but cannot settle unequal-LN D/E. Backtesting rejected a general shallow-rectifier override: it won 0/6 same-rate Adagrad history comparisons. Optimizer-type/rate-matched lab comparisons gave shallow wins in 6/7 Adam-family pairs but 0/2 SGD pairs, with no Adagrad pairs or fully optimizer-matched pairs. Thus the gold supports a local D/E exception, not a validated general mechanism.

The decisive miss was D beating B despite equal GELU activation and three LayerNorms. I assumed D’s unnormalized prefix would irreversibly attenuate input dependence; later normalization can rescale those representations and alter gradient conditioning, so that assumption was unjustified. This is a plausible mechanism, not established by the ordinal gold. K1006 and K1039 supported other comparisons but did not resolve D/B; K1022 explicitly excludes univariate regression. A low-rate SGD, equal-LN, same-activation later-placement heuristic hit 2/2 eligible historical pairs (q_fc0253, q_ada9c2), but neither reproduces this terminal-normalized contrast. Across 988 univariate lab candidates, no eligible matched placement pairs existed. Evidence is insufficient for a general rule or identified reversal regime.

The only error was C versus E: shallow, unnormalized GELU beat deeper residual SiLU with one middle LN. I overextended K1006’s normalization tendency and treated residual connections as additional support, despite K1015’s warning. K1008 and K1022 helped order the leading candidates. Backtesting found no exact depth-2/plain/zero-LN versus depth-3/residual/one-LN smooth pair at matched optimizer/rate in history or lab. Broader comparisons favored the residual candidate in all 7 historical pairs and all 33 lab pairs across 7 sets, but none used RMSprop. Thus the gold exposes an unsupported optimizer-regime extrapolation, not a validated reverse rule. Target-specific fitting or RMSprop–normalization interaction remains untested; ranking alone cannot identify the mechanism.

Shared SGD recipes made architecture the deciding factor. K1039 supported the normalized rectifier candidates over SiLU C and D, including E despite its one-fewer-LN gap versus C. K1006 weakly supported A’s three LNs over B’s two and B over E, but did not establish a deterministic ordering. D’s deep, plain, zero-LN SiLU stack was least favorable for rapid fitting; K1038 supplied task-scoped caution rather than an automatic freezing rule. The gold ranking agrees with these tendencies, but this single result does not isolate normalization, activation, depth, or residual effects.

I over-applied K1039’s rectifier tendency: B beat A despite two fewer LNs in A, and C beat E despite E’s rectifier activation. B’s repeated normalization and C’s normalized residual paths plausibly improved nonlinear fitting under slow momentum SGD; gradient measurements are unavailable, so this is not an established mechanism. K1006’s architecture-bundle caution helped; K1074 only supports B versus C, not B versus A. Backtesting a replacement “more-LN smooth beats fewer-LN rectifier” rule failed: 24/47 historical comparisons across 20 questions; B-like cases won 6/11, C-like 1/3. The lab contained no eligible same-rate/momentum univariate SGD comparisons. No general replacement rule is supported.

I misplaced C, causing all three inversions. Its residual SiLU network evidently learned useful structure despite zero LayerNorm; my assumed activation attenuation was not sufficient to predict slow learning over 1024 RMSprop steps. Residual signal preservation is a plausible explanation, not a measured mechanism. K1006/K1008 were overextended into normalization-first and rectifier-first rankings; K1008 requires equal LN counts. K1015 correctly cautions against ordering architectural bundles. Backtests reject a general C-style advantage: matched optimizer/rate/budget history favored zero-LN smooth residuals over zero-LN rectifiers in 2/8 pairs and normalized smooth rivals in 3/11. Full-recipe lab comparisons favored them in 20/80 pairs across six sets, with no matching RMSprop comparisons. No tested replacement rule emerged.

I over-weighted LayerNorm count: E beat B despite fewer norms, and C beat A despite having none. E’s deeper nonlinear composition and C’s residual signal preservation are plausible explanations, but ordinal gold cannot establish either mechanism. K1006 explicitly warned against LN-first ranking; I failed to honor that warning. K1074 helped prioritize depth but does not cover E versus B because E has fewer norms. Backtesting found no matching deep/fewer-LN comparison. For zero-LN residual versus shallow one-LN plain models, low-progress Adam-family history favored residuals in 0/2 comparisons. Broader same-type/rate adaptive lab checks yielded 1/1 win below Δ=.1 and 0/1 above it. These sparse, conflicting results support no general correction rule.

I overextended conditional preferences into a complete architecture score. A’s win fits K1018, but B beating D/E/C shows that smoothness, extra LN, and terminal LN cannot order these bundles. I incorrectly favored C’s terminal LN despite K1061’s SGD-specific scope, and underweighted K1006’s warning against LN-count ranking. Backtesting shared adaptive optimizer/type, rate, and budget on ≥8-feature XOR found smooth-residual versus plain-rectifier wins in 10/14 high-progress history pairs and 9/9 lab pairs; low-progress results reversed to 2/7 and 0/4. Neither source supplied eligible same-depth plain-rectifier normalization contrasts explaining B<E<C. The missed effect is architecture-bundle dependence; its causal mechanism remains unestablished, so no tested rule predicts the complete gold order.

I overvalued C’s residual signal propagation. D beat C despite equal depth, width, activation, LN count, and optimizer: their normalization placement and skip topology must be treated as a bundle. D normalizes the first hidden block; C delays normalization and repeatedly carries unnormalized activations through skips. Better conditioning for this target is plausible, but unmeasured. K1006 warned against precisely this architecture shortcut; K1016 correctly discouraged capacity-based ranking. Backtesting found only two comparable smooth-SGD univariate lab pairs, both favoring residual networks, with activation/placement confounds. History supplied no exact matched comparison. Thus neither a plain-over-residual rule nor a placement mechanism is established; the missed ordering remains recipe-specific.

B and D led correctly, but E beat both A and C. I overextended K1074’s deep-network preference to A despite its single LN and several unnormalized SiLU blocks, and assumed plain GELU would beat residual SiLU without supporting evidence. E’s shorter residual path plausibly preserves input-dependent signal better at this small learning rate, but that mechanism is unverified. K1006’s warning against architecture scoring was more relevant; K1016 correctly discouraged capacity-based ranking. Backtesting found one comparable historical shallow/deep, one-LN residual-smooth pair: it favored deep, contradicting a shallow-first rule. The lab contained no eligible matched pairs for either proposed effect. No tested general rule supports these two corrected orders.

The only missed comparison was D beating B: the unnormalized LeakyReLU network outweighed B’s single LayerNorm and SiLU activation. Rectifiers plausibly preserve stronger input-dependent features during short, low-rate fitting, but this mechanism is unmeasured. K1074 helped select A; K1008 supported matched activation comparisons, not D versus B. I overextended K1006’s conditional normalization preference. Backtesting a broader shallow-zero-LN rectifier preference at shared adaptive type/rate and Δ<.1 gave 5 wins/7 history comparisons across 5 questions, including two counterexamples. Lab had no exact plain-zero-LN versus plain-one-LN controls; broader fewer-LN rectifier comparisons won only 6/12 across 8 low-progress sets. No general override is justified.

B beat A despite equal LN counts: the shallow rectifier preference did not settle a comparison that also changed depth and residual connections. B’s deeper residual GELU network plausibly supplied more useful nonlinear features while preserving signal propagation, but the revealed ranking cannot identify that mechanism. I overextended K1008; its activation tendency explicitly excludes residual/topology changes. K1074 supplied a relevant normalized-depth prior that I overlooked. Backtesting matched optimizer/rate, normalized deep-residual versus shallow recipes found 19/23 wins across 15 historical questions, but only 9/14 lab wins across 12 sets. The lab contained no exact Adagrad smooth-deep versus shallow-rectifier comparison. These results support reconsidering B, not a universal depth-first rule.

I mistook normalization count and depth for a generalization ranking. Gold instead favors C’s residual SiLU bundle, then A’s unnormalized residual ReLU, with heavily normalized B/E last. K1006 and K1009 explicitly warned against the additive architecture score I effectively used; K1056’s smooth-activation tendency deserved more weight. Backtesting shared-optimizer/rate, equal-residual-status piecewise comparisons at nominal Δ=.01–.1 favored smooth activations in 20/29 history pairs across nine questions and 15/21 lab pairs across six sets. However, fewer-LN residual rectifiers won 0/6 comparable lab pairs in one set, contradicting a blanket explanation for A<D<B. Confidence calibration or nuisance-feature fitting could explain this instance, but neither mechanism is established by the revealed ranking.

All candidates shared Adagrad lr=.001 and the same budget, so optimizer progress did not distinguish them. K1006 supported B’s heavily normalized architecture as a conditional preference; K1008 supported A over its activation-only SiLU twin C. K1074 supported normalized depth-four D over shallow C and E at equal nominal progress. A versus D was less directly supported because depth and activation changed together. The gold order agrees with these tendencies, but this single result does not establish an additive normalization, activation, and depth score.

All candidates shared plain SGD and a short budget. C’s terminal-block pre-LN favored it over the other deep plain networks (K1059). A and B’s shallow residual paths favored them over D and E, whose deeper plain stacks ended with an unnormalized block (K1061). A versus B and E versus D were weaker architectural judgments, not established activation or placement laws. K1006 helped keep LN count from becoming an additive ranking score. The gold order supports this specific bundle comparison but adds no tested general rule.

K1074 supported the deep, fully normalized A over shallow rivals at equal training rate and budget. K1039 supported shallow rectifier B over smooth D despite B having one fewer LN. D over zero-LN C/E was a less certain architecture judgment, not a validated LN-count rule; K1006 cautioned against treating normalization as an additive score. C over E reflected the plausible benefit of its shallow residual path, but skips and activation changed together. K1016 helped avoid ranking by width. The result supports this bundled ordering without establishing a new general rule.

B’s moderately deep, early-normalized GELU bundle beat D’s deeper, more-normalized LeakyReLU bundle; A’s shallow normalized residual SiLU bundle beat E’s unnormalized ReLU network. I incorrectly treated rectifier activation as decisive across changed topology and LN count, outside K1008’s scope. K1006 and K1080 warned against that inference; K1016 also discouraged capacity-based ranking. A shallower-normalized-smooth preference won only 5/15 comparable history pairs, losing the sole RMSprop comparison. A-like versus E-like bundles won 3/5 history pairs, with no RMSprop examples. The lab supplied no matching RMSprop architecture pairs at T1024. Thus normalization-assisted signal propagation is plausible, but neither the causal mechanism nor a general rule is established.

B’s one-LN plain LeakyReLU bundle beat E’s two-LN residual ReLU bundle despite identical depth, width, and Adam recipe. I overvalued residual signal propagation; carrying distractor features through skips could hurt generalization, but that mechanism is unverified. K1018 and K1065 helped place D and C; neither justified E above B. K1006 explicitly warned against ranking changed architecture bundles by normalization count. Backtesting a plain-over-residual rule at equal depth, with rectifiers and no more LN, contradicted it: history gave only 1/10 plain wins; lab gave 0/18 across five sets. No lab pairs matched the relevant high-progress adaptive regime. This is a bundle-specific exception, not evidence for a general plain-network preference.

E beat A despite one fewer LN and less depth. I implicitly rewarded A's normalized depth, contrary to K1006's warning against an architecture score. E's shorter LeakyReLU residual path plausibly preserves stronger features and enables faster fitting at lr=3e-5; this mechanism remains unmeasured. K1001/K1012 helped identify D's large progress advantage. K1008 supplies only equal-LN activation evidence, not an E>A rule. Backtesting shallow normalized rectifier versus deeper smooth residual at matched low Adam-family rates found zero qualifying lab pairs and one historical comparison, which reversed the proposed preference (q_718119). Broader equal-LN lab comparisons favored rectifiers 2/3 below Delta=.1 but 0/2 above it, all architecture-confounded. No general rule is justified.

E’s deeper plain ReLU bundle beat B’s residual LeakyReLU bundle despite equal LN counts and identical SGD settings. I overcredited residual optimization; K1039 supported rectifiers over smooth activations, not B over E. K1006 correctly warned against topology scoring. Better nonlinear feature refinement through E’s normalized plain stack is plausible, but unmeasured; depth, width, activation and LN placement remain confounded. Backtesting found one comparable historical pair: plain won (1 hit, 0 misses). Exact deep, ≥3-LN lab comparisons numbered zero. Broader normalized-rectifier SGD comparisons favored deeper plain univariate models in 13/16 pairs across eight sets, but only 2/6 multivariate pairs. These dependent, mismatched comparisons do not establish a reliable E-over-B rule.

The easy quadratic target favored E’s shallow, zero-LN residual GELU network with AdamW at .001. A’s normalized residual network had enough Adagrad progress at .001 to beat C, despite C’s larger nominal displacement. C’s .0003 AdamW recipe then beat low-rate D and B. K1002 helped identify B’s undertraining risk; K1012 and K1006 cautioned against mechanically sorting displacement or LN count. K1074 did not justify preferring normalized depth over E because the learning-rate gap was too large. This result supports the existing scoped guidance, not a new general rule.

The decisive reversal was D<E: the residual ReLU network outperformed the deeper plain SiLU network despite having two fewer layer norms. Preserved input-dependent features and faster rectifier fitting are plausible explanations, not measured mechanisms. I overextended K1074’s normalized-depth preference beyond its shallow-rival scope; K1006 explicitly warns against ordering these bundles by LN count, and K1008 does not settle unequal-LN/topology comparisons. Backtesting found no exact-scope historical or lab comparisons. Broadening to residual rectifiers versus plain smooth networks with more LN yielded one low-rate historical comparison, which favored the smooth network; three higher-rate lab comparisons favored rectifiers, across three sets with other knobs confounded. These results do not support a general D-over-E rule.

The sole error was C versus D: D’s deeper SiLU network with two later LNs beat C’s shallower network with three early LNs. A plausible explanation is that early normalization changes input-dependent feature geometry, whereas later normalization rescales already transformed features; this mechanism remains unmeasured. K1039 helped place the rectifiers first, but cannot order two SiLU candidates. K1006 correctly warned against counting LNs; my prediction nevertheless favored C’s normalization/depth bundle without sufficient evidence. Backtesting a fewer-LN preference on shared-rate/momentum, equal-width, plain smooth univariate SGD history yielded only 1/7 wins across five questions. The lab contained no eligible comparable pairs. Thus this inversion supports a local placement/topology effect, not a validated general rule.

q_2dd5df.comment: The missed comparisons were B<D and C<E. I overvalued D’s residual depth and normalization relative to B’s plain, middle-LN architecture, and implicitly favored E’s smooth activation over C’s residual rectifier. Plausible mechanisms are B’s effective nonlinear composition and C’s preservation of input-dependent scale through skips, but neither is established by the revealed ranking. K1066 supports D over shallow rivals, not over depth-3 B; K1061’s strongest evidence is SGD-scoped. K1015 cautioned against my topology shortcut. Excluding this question, plain normalized smooth networks beat more-normalized deep residual smooth rivals in only 2/10 history contrasts across seven questions; lab results were optimizer-dependent. No exact prior C/E control was found. No general replacement rule is validated.
